openers.horizons-and-the-soil-profile: Dig a pit almost anywhere and its walls show bands, each one a layer with its own story. The upper layer is richest in organic matter and microorganisms, and most of the soil's biological activity happens there. Beneath it lies a mix of sand, silt and clay with far less organic matter. Water percolating down strips material from the upper layers and deposits it lower down, so each band gains or loses its own ingredients. This chapter names those bands, from a surface layer of plant residues to the barely altered material above bedrock, and shows how soil scientists describe them and use them to classify soils.

soil-form-021.title: Topsoil, the thin living layer that feeds plants
soil-form-021.text: One inch (2.5 cm) of topsoil can take 500 to 1,000 years to form. The United States loses almost 3 tons of it per acre every year. Topsoil is the upper layer of soil, richest in soil organic matter and microorganisms, where most of the soil's biological activity takes place. It is a mix of mineral particles and soil organic matter, usually 5–10 inches (13–25 cm) deep. The water and air it holds encourage that activity. Roots concentrate here, because plants draw most of their nutrients from this layer. Bacteria and fungi break down organic material, while insects aerate and turn the soil. Its depth runs from the surface to the first densely packed layer, described in {{ref:soil-form-023}}. Classification systems label it as one of two horizons, covered in {{ref:soil-form-006}} and {{ref:soil-form-008}}. More soil organic matter helps its particles hold together. Dried-out topsoil loses much of its volume, and the wind carries it off more easily. The optimum {{ref:soil-fert-184}} for UK topsoil is less than 20:1. Today, use and erosion strip topsoil faster than new soil forms. Cover crops, {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-099}} and windbreaks slow the loss and keep it fertile.

soil-form-023.title: Subsoil, where the rain drops its cargo
soil-form-023.text: Rain does more than wet the ground. It carries weathering products such as clay minerals and iron oxides downward, dissolved or as fine suspended particles, and most of them settle in the subsoil. Subsoil is the layer beneath {{ref:soil-form-021}}, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less soil organic matter. With so little of it, the subsoil's color comes mainly from iron oxides. Physical, chemical and biological activity cluster its particles into a definite arrangement, and that sets it apart from the barely altered substratum below. It is not sterile, but it holds few soil organisms compared with the rich layer above. Most soil mapping systems give it the letter B, with a substratum lettered C beneath; {{ref:soil-form-010}} and {{ref:soil-form-011}} return to both. Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments. Builders have used clay-rich subsoil for millennia, as adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub.

soil-form-001.title: Soil morphology: describing a soil by eye and hand
soil-form-001.text: Dokuchaev's team noticed something striking. Profiles with similar horizons turned up hundreds of kilometers apart, wherever climate and vegetation were similar. Observing like that is soil morphology, the branch of soil science that describes soils technically, above all their texture, color, structure and consistence. Nineteenth-century agro-geologists, studying soils in natural settings, were the first to do it scientifically. Once soils were seen as independent natural bodies, morphology became a way to judge the combined influence of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. Official guidelines first appeared in the 1930s, from Charles Kellogg and the USDA in the United States and from G.R. Clarke in the United Kingdom. Today a describer works in the field on several horizons exposed by a pit, a push tube or an auger. Many US soil scientists record site, horizons, color, texture and structure on a standard USDA-NRCS field sheet. Structure is best judged fairly dry, because moist clumps swell and press together. Together with the study of how soils form and how they are classified, morphology belongs to pedology.

soil-form-033.title: Eluviation: how percolating water empties the upper soil
soil-form-033.text: Where more rain falls than evaporates, water keeps moving down through the soil, and it takes things with it. That removal of soil material from upper layers by percolating water is eluviation. It carries mineral and organic colloids, particles fine enough to stay suspended in water. That sets it apart from {{ref:soil-form-050}}, a distinct soil-building mechanism. Acid conditions speed it up, because organic acids make iron and aluminum more soluble. {{ref:soil-form-061}} is the extreme case, stripping out sesquioxides, the oxides of iron and aluminum. The layer that loses material is an eluvial horizon. It may be a light-colored zone at the base of the surface mineral horizon, labelled Ae. Where the process is most intense, it forms a separate layer beneath, lettered E and described in {{ref:soil-form-009}}. Some sources count both of these layers as the eluvial zone. What leaves must land somewhere. The material builds up lower down as an illuvial deposit, the process of {{ref:soil-form-032}}. On a slope the exchange also runs downhill: upper facets lose salts while lower facets gain them.

soil-form-017.title: Diagnostic horizons, the layers that decide a soil's name
soil-form-017.text: To name a soil, a classifier checks each of its horizons against a list of criteria. A diagnostic horizon is one defined by such a set of criteria. Its presence or absence at a given depth decides which taxonomic unit the soil belongs to. The WRB lists 40 of them. The WRB, {{ref:soil-class-006}} and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} all work this way, while the German system defines soils by whole sequences of horizons. Diagnostic horizons usually carry names rather than symbols, such as the spodic horizon or the one in {{ref:soil-form-031}}. The USDA system separates diagnostic surface horizons, covered in {{ref:soil-form-018}}, from subsurface ones. Among those are the spodic and oxic horizons and the clay-rich layer in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. Most systems also use other soil characteristics to define their units.

soil-form-006.title: The O horizon, a blanket of leaves and needles
soil-form-006.text: Leaves, conifer needles, twigs, mosses and lichens gather on many soils and slowly decompose in place. The result is the O horizon: a surface layer of organic material built from plant residues, not mixed into the mineral soil and not waterlogged for long periods. The WRB counts material as organic when it holds at least 20% organic carbon by weight. The upper part is often barely decomposed litter, while the lower part may be strongly humified, broken down into dark, stable organic material. The Australian system splits it into O1 and O2 on that basis. It also keeps loose leaf litter, which has no weathered mineral particles, out of the soil altogether. Organisms in the O horizon break down the residues and release nutrients. Strong acidity, cold or pollution slow them, so undecomposed material piles up over the mineral soil. Though it forms on top, an O horizon can be buried at depth by landslides, floods or wind-blown dust.

soil-form-008.title: The A horizon, where life and minerals mix
soil-form-008.text: Earthworms, potworms, arthropods, nematodes, fungi, bacteria and archaea crowd around plant roots in the A horizon, which is why some call it the biomantle. It is the uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified soil organic matter is intimately mixed with mineral material. Often called topsoil, it holds dark, decomposed soil organic matter. Burrowing animals stir it into the mineral matter, a mixing described in {{ref:soil-bio-047}}. The original rock structure is fully or largely gone. Biological activity reaches much deeper, though, so it cannot be the chief test, and A horizons are defined mostly relative to the layers beneath. Layers changed by plowing or pasturing count as A horizons, and the suffix p marks plowed ones. The Australian system divides it into A1, dark and most biologically active, A2, paler, and A3, a transition to the layer below.

soil-form-009.title: The E horizon, a pale layer washed clean
soil-form-009.text: Old, well-developed soils often hide a band paler than the layers around it. That is the E horizon, E for eluviated. It is a mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminum, soil organic matter or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz. Where eluviation is pronounced, it appears below the A horizon and above a layer lettered B, covered in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. It differs from that lower layer by higher color value or lower chroma, coarser texture, or both. Sometimes it takes the color of its own sand and silt. The lost substances first had to form or collect in place, so an E horizon marks an advanced stage of soil development. In gravelly soils, burrowing animals commonly leave a stone layer near its base. The Australian system does not use E; it labels such washed-out layers A or B with the suffix e.

soil-form-025.title: Hardpans, the buried floors that stop roots
soil-form-025.text: Some soils have a floor that roots and water cannot get through. A hardpan is a dense, largely water-impervious layer, usually lying just below the topsoil. Some form naturally, when deposits such as dissolved silica, iron oxides or calcium carbonate fuse and bind the soil particles. Acidic soils suffer most, because iron and calcium salts form hard complexes with soil particles under acid conditions. Other pans are man-made, compacted by repeated plowing, especially with moldboard plows, by heavy traffic or by pollution. Clay-rich soils compact easily, and sodium in wastewater can bind clay into a local pan, a common cause of septic system failure. Hardpans impede drainage and restrict roots on farms and in gardens. A broadfork, digging fork, spade or tractor-drawn chisel plow can break them. Manure, compost or peat improve drainage and encourage earthworms that slowly break pans. Lime and gypsum help with harder ones, though amendments may take years. {{ref:soil-water-242}} turns irreversibly into an ironstone hardpan when wetted and dried again and again.

soil-form-032.title: Illuviation: where washed-down material comes to rest
soil-form-032.text: Everything water carries out of an upper layer has to stop somewhere. Illuviation is that stopping: the deposition in a lower layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above. It is the matching half of eluviation. Illuvium includes soil organic matter, silicate clay and hydrous oxides of iron and aluminum. These collect in subsoil horizons lettered B, the zones of illuviation, described in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. The movement is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the sideways transfer by running water. It works in two ways. In mechanical illuviation, a drier horizon draws water from percolating suspensions by capillarity, the pull of water into fine pores. Fine coatings are left along the channels, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-068}}. In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried down by percolating water are deposited where the chemistry of the soil changes, especially its pH and its {{ref:soil-chem-123}}. Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough washed-in clay are the ones named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and gathers in the subsoil.

soil-form-010.title: The B horizon, the soil's collecting zone
soil-form-010.text: Brown or reddish, the B horizon takes its color from iron oxides, because it holds less soil organic matter than the A horizon above. It is a subsurface mineral horizon, formed below a horizon lettered A, E, H or O. Its original rock structure is largely gone, and soil-forming processes have altered or enriched its material. It is commonly called subsoil. Where it gathers material moving down from the A and E horizons, it is also called the illuvial horizon. Its marks include residual oxides or clay minerals, lost carbonates or gypsum, and washed-in clay, iron, aluminum, organic material, carbonates, gypsum or silica. It generally has a structure or consistency that differs from the layers above and below. Gleying alone does not make a B horizon, nor do carbonates cut off from a genetic horizon above. The Australian system splits it into B1, transitional from A, B2, with concentrated clay or oxides, and B3, transitional to the C or D horizon.

soil-form-011.title: The C horizon, raw material soil barely touched
soil-form-011.text: Below the layers that soil-forming processes have reshaped lies material it has barely touched. The C horizon is that layer: anything above hard bedrock that those processes have little affected and that lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons. It includes sediments, saprolite and soft bedrock that a spade can dig when moist and that usually slakes, crumbling in water, within 24 hours. It forms in deposits such as loess, flood deposits and landslides, or by weathering of bedrock in place. Unless a change in parent material separates them, a break covered in {{ref:soil-form-015}}, it resembles the parent material of the soil above, though C material may differ. Plant roots can penetrate it, so it is an important growing medium. It may be enriched with carbonates and other soluble compounds washed down from above. Layers cemented by silica, carbonates or gypsum stay C unless soil-forming processes have clearly affected them; then they become B horizons.

soil-form-034.title: Cryoturbation: frost that churns the soil
soil-form-034.text: In the coldest soils, the ground will not keep its layers in order. Cryoturbation, or frost churning, mixes material from different horizons, down to bedrock, through repeated freezing and thawing in soils of {{ref:soil-env-129}}, where the ground below stays frozen. It occurs to some degree in most soils of the {{ref:soil-class-096}} order, a name from the Latin gelare, to freeze. In autumn, freezing forms wedges of ice in the most erodible parts of the parent rock, the subject of {{ref:soil-form-036}}. In summer, the part that thaws, described in {{ref:soil-env-146}}, lets loosened material move both down and up. Moisture moves from the warm surface toward the cold, frozen ground below. It dries the upper soil into a granular structure laced with lenses of ice. Coarse material separates from fine, producing {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. Frost churning is the dominant force in that thawing layer and tends to make it uniform. It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys. Turbels show it in over one-third of the thawing layer, with distorted boundaries between horizons; Orthels show less. In frost boils it can bring base-rich water to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients.

soil-form-002.title: The soil profile, a record read from the top down
soil-form-002.text: Going down a soil profile means going back in time. Like layers of sediment, its horizons record past events. A soil profile is a vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface. Formally, it is one face of the three-dimensional block described in {{ref:soil-form-003}}. Soil scientists expose a profile by digging a pit or extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons. Some soils, such as those of the {{ref:soil-class-094}} order, have only one horizon or none. Young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces are examples. Wind or running water can strip the upper horizons and bury them downslope, a natural process that {{ref:soil-agri-095}} aggravates. Major earthworks or regular deep plowing can leave a soil almost without distinct horizons. The horizons also hold clues to the past. Pollen, testate amoebae and plant remains can reveal changes in climate or land use, and large pieces of charcoal allow radiocarbon dating.

soil-form-024.title: The solum, the part of the soil that formed together
soil-form-024.text: A 10 cm surface layer on bedrock can be a complete solum, while fresh alluvium has none at all. The solum is the upper part of a soil, its surface and subsoil layers, developed under the same soil-forming conditions. In horizon terms it covers the A, E and B horizons, the blended layers between them and some O horizons. Its base is relatively unweathered parent material. Layers where carbonate or salt accumulated belong too, if they formed at least partly in the same period. A solum has no minimum or maximum thickness. Its lower limit should relate to how deep the roots of perennial plants are expected to reach, though in some soils it can only be set arbitrarily. Hardened carbonate or gleying many meters down is hard to count, since such deep features may be relict or geological rather than products of soil development. The living part of the soil stays largely within the solum and is most prominent in the A horizon.

soil-form-007.title: The H horizon, peat that sits in water
soil-form-007.text: Not every organic layer stays dry. The H horizon is an organic layer, generally peat, that is saturated with water for long periods or has been artificially drained. In the WRB an H layer is saturated for more than 30 consecutive days in most years, or drained. An O horizon, by contrast, is saturated for no more than 30 days and not drained. Many H horizons consist mainly of sphagnum mosses. After drainage, O horizons may form on top of them. The Australian system calls these waterlogged layers P, for peats, with at least 12 to 18% organic carbon depending on clay content.

soil-form-012.title: The R layer, bedrock at the bottom of the pit
soil-form-012.text: At the base of the profile, the spade stops. The R layer is the hard, consolidated bedrock beneath the soil: granite, basalt, quartzite, or hard limestone or sandstone. It is too coherent to dig by hand with a spade, and air-dry chunks do not slake in water within 24 hours. Its few small cracks let few roots in. Where no change in parent material separates them, the R layer resembles the parent material of the solum above.

soil-form-004.title: Horizon designations, a soil's layers written in code
soil-form-004.text: Ah-E-Bt1-2Bt2-2BwC-3C1-3C2 looks like a serial number. It is a whole soil profile written in horizon designations, the code of letters and numbers that names each horizon. A capital letter gives the master horizon, such as O, A, E, B, C or R. Lowercase suffixes add details of how the layer formed, and several may be combined. Some master horizons, including O, B and L, must always carry one. Numbers do two jobs. A number in front marks a change in parent material, covered in {{ref:soil-form-015}}. A number behind splits one horizon into subdivisions, such as Bt1, Bt2 and Bt3. Hyphens join the horizons of a profile into one string. That short notation summarizes color, size, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules or concretions. The world has many systems of horizon symbols, and the same horizon may be labelled differently in each. No system is more correct than another. Because their symbols are defined differently, though, the systems cannot be mixed.
